title: The War at Home
sub: Grades 5–8 · Social Studies · One family on the home front
objective: Students learn how the Second World War changed women’s work in Britain, then follow the war into the home of Violet Dina Want, a London machinist and mother of four. They sort the exhibition’s sources into primary and secondary, reason from a museum note to the earliest date an event could have happened, and ask what a museum chooses to keep.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: Much of a war happens to people who never appear in a textbook. Reading their letters, photographs and family stories, and asking what is missing, is how historians find them.

materials: Poster 1’s *Women in wartime* panel and poster 2, on a screen, or page 3 of this plan
questions: Poster 1 says women did jobs “previously done by men.” Which jobs? What might have happened to those jobs after the war?
Why might a family keep letters that a bomb had damaged?
The biography was written down by Violet’s family. What might a family remember that an archive would not, and the other way round?
Whose wartime stories would be missing if nobody had collected them at the time?
questionsLabel: Questions to ask in front of the posters
connection: **In the exhibition,** poster 1’s *Women in wartime* panel links to the Imperial War Museum’s Women’s Work Collection; the *Violet’s Life* room tells her story stop by stop. **In the display case,** the family’s bomb-damaged letters.

steps.title: One object
script: Show the record of the display case’s one object: *“Original Blitz bomb-damaged family letters from Violet Dina Want’s estate.”* The letters are not transcribed, so nobody visiting the exhibition can read them. Ask: *“This is the one object in the exhibition’s display case. What could these letters tell a historian? What could they never tell?”* Keep the answers on the board.

steps.purpose: Set the two halves of the lesson: women’s work, and the war reaching home.

steps.title: Women in wartime
script: **The work.** Read poster 1’s *Women in wartime* panel aloud (page 3): men aged 18 to 41 went to the navy and army, and women took their jobs, in weapons factories and in the Land Army on farms. Add its note: the Imperial War Museum began collecting women’s war work in 1917, the year it was founded.

screen.text: In the Second World War, British men aged 18 to 41 were needed in the navy and army, which took them away from their jobs. To fill the shortage, women were recruited for jobs previously done by men. Women worked in the factories, constructing weapons, and many others joined the Land Army to work on farms.

steps.purpose: Learn what changed for women’s work, and why.
students: Which two kinds of work does the panel name?

steps.title: The war reaches home
script: **The home.** Turn to poster 2. Violet, born in London in 1907, left school at 14 to work as a piecework machinist, married in 1928, and had four children, born between 1929 and 1942. Read its lines on the Blitz: the bombing destroyed the family’s homes and scattered them across the South of England.

Then tell the next sentence of the poster plainly: a V-1 “doodlebug” bomb exploded nearby, shattering every window in Violet’s home, and her mother was killed when her house collapsed. Give the room’s museum note: *The first V-1 to hit London fell on June 13, 1944.* Ask what that lets us work out. Note what the poster does **not** say: what work, if any, Violet did in the war.

screen.text: Before World War II, Violet’s extended family lived in close-knit neighboring streets, but the heavy bombing during the Blitz destroyed their homes, scattering them across the South of England.
screen.cite: Poster 2 · Biography of a Working Class Woman

steps.purpose: See the war as one family lived it.
students: What did the bombing do to Violet’s family?
What else would you want to know?

steps.title: Primary or secondary?
script: **The sources.** A **primary** source was made at the time, by people who were there; a **secondary** source tells about the past afterwards. Violet’s biography was written down by her family later. Ask: which kind shows what people *felt*, and which what *happened next*?

steps.purpose: Sort the exhibition’s own sources, and see that each kind shows something different.
students: Which of these was made at the time?
Which tells the most? Which can we trust most?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. All three read the same panel, the same lines of Violet’s biography and the same four sources.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Read the *Women in wartime* panel and fill in what changed, sort four sources as primary or secondary, and explain one way the war reached Violet’s home.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Compare what the panel shows about all women with what Violet’s story shows about one, reason from the V-1 note to the earliest date her home could have been hit, and read the letters’ record as a historian.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Ask why a museum collected women’s war work so soon, decide which claims in Violet’s biography could be checked and how, and write a museum label for the letters using only what is known.

steps.purpose: Read the panel, the biography and the sources at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three read the war through women’s work and Violet’s home.

steps.title: Look back
script: Ask the objectives back: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down; ask one student to answer each aloud, and a Red Level student the last.

steps.title: For boys, for girls
script: Close with poster 1’s own question: *“Many women in wartime did jobs that people had said only men could do. What jobs or roles do people still sometimes say are “for boys” or “for girls,” and what do you think about that?”*
